A historical overview giving a moral rationale for the fall of the Shang and the rise of the Western Zhou: the King says that drinking wine in excess made the Shang lose the Mandate of Heaven, grace and the army, while the Kings of Zhou do not drink excessively even ceremonially. The King then commands Yu to support him and to work official service throughout days. Content E55: Note Type

the English translation of the Da Yu ding inscription E33: Linguistic Object English E56: Language
It was in the ninth month when the King was at Zongzhou. The King charged Yu saying, "Yu! Shining King Wen received the great mandate from Heaven. When King Wu succeeded Wen, he created a state, opening hidden lands, possessing all the four quarters, and setting right their peoples. In ceremonial affairs involving wine, oh! - he permitted no excess; at sacrificial rites, he permitted no drunkenness. Hence Heaven in its greatness watched closely over its sons and protected the former Kings in their possession of the four quarters. I have heard that the Yin loss of the mandate was due to the fact that its greater and lesser lords and the many officials assisting the Yin sank into drunkenness and so were bereft of their city. You have helped me from the hazy dawn of my youth: When I was engaged in my youthful studies, you never coerced me but always helped me. Now I am attempting to emulate and grasp the upright virtue of King Wen, and charge the many officials as he did. Now I charge you to assist Rong in attending to the constancy of harmonious virtue: be assiduous in remonstrating with me from dawn to dusk serving in awe of Heaven's awesomeness." The King said, "Oh! I charge you Yu to emulate your late grandfather Nan Gong, whom you succeed." The King said, "Yu, assist me by overseeing until death the affairs of war. Assiduously remonstrate and upbraid me. From dawn to dusk help me to govern the four quarters and follow the former Kings in receiving charge of the people and the lands. I give to you a flask of sacrificial liquors, ceremonial cap, robes, kneepads, and sandals, and a chariot with horse. I present to you the banner of your late grandfather Nan Gong for you to lead in hunting. I give to you four estate officials and 659 servant from charioteers to common peasants. I give you thirteen officials of the rank of King's officers to guard your borders, and along with them 1,050 servants. Move them promptly from their current lands." The King said, "Yu! Be attentive to your government and do not disobey my charge." In gratitude for the favors of the King, Yu casts this precious cauldron for his late grandfather Nan Gong. It was in the King's twenty-third sacrificial year. Minford, "The Triumph: A Heritage of Sorts", China Heritage Quarterly 19 (2009) E31: Document

Xiao Yu ding E22: Human-Made Object
Two grounds are given in the article. First, the Xiao Yu ding, which was discovered alongside the Da Yu ding, mentions sacrifices made to King Wen, King Wu and King Cheng, which places it in the following reign. Second, the design of the Da Yu ding compares well with other bronze artifacts of that period. The attribution is therefore inferential, not documentary, and is recorded as an assignment rather than as a direct property of the production. Statement E55: Note Type
